Building in public · MIT / Apache-2.0 primitives where noted
01 / Values

Infrastructure should serve its operators—not strand them.

The shared core stays understandable, replaceable, and useful long after a vendor moves on.

P—01⌁

Open at the core

New primitives target permissive MIT or Apache-2.0 licensing where appropriate. Interfaces stay public so the community can inspect, extend, and replace components.

P—02⟲

Right to repair

Modular drivers and portable contracts make practical support possible across old machines, new silicon, and equipment its original vendor abandoned.

P—03◇

Private by design

Local-first operation, least-privilege access, signed changes, and verifiable evidence. Your infrastructure does not require a permanent cloud dependency.

P—04⋈

Interoperable

Linux, macOS, Windows, embedded systems, and vendor appliances can participate through narrow contracts—not forced rewrites or a single runtime.

02 / Shape

Not another kernel.
Not another monolith.

A common substrate becomes different products through explicit profiles. Nothing is bundled everywhere simply because it exists.

ExperienceAgent and human interfaces built for safe, explainable operation.
WorkloadsExisting services, containers, media tools, and compute runtimes.
OperationsIdentity, topology, updates, health, policy, and reproducible lifecycle actions.
SystemsDebian, macOS, embedded firmware, vendor Linux, and future community ports.
HardwareFrom Raspberry Pi and studio Macs to bare metal, GPUs, and shop-floor controllers.
  • +
    Meet systems where they areAdopt existing machines before asking anyone to reimage them.
  • +
    Separate observation from authorityDiscovery can report what exists. Policy decides who may act.
  • +
    Make every automated action a runbookPlans, receipts, rollback points, and evidence instead of invisible magic.
  • +
    Replace parts without replacing the wholeStable contracts keep the ecosystem loosely coupled.

Composable deployment profiles

The open core includes the profile format, authoring, enforcement, application, and evidence collection. Anyone can build or use community and FPL-published open baselines, including STIG-aligned profiles.

Fleet / cloud

Operate the machine estate

Mycelium for fleet operations, Shroud for workload isolation, and storage primitives form the cloud and fleet core.

Interactive / physical

Connect people to place

On-prem profiles can add Unibus and Canvas for USB, HID, MIDI, media, studio, and machine-floor interaction.

FPL enterprise assurance

Support the operating program

Validated and signed profile releases, supported qualification matrices, control-to-evidence mappings, regression testing, implementation guidance, update cadence, SLA support, and customer-specific regulated or classified tailoring.

03 / Where it grows

One operating philosophy. Very different rooms.

The substrate is shared; each environment keeps the tools, policies, and hardware that make it distinct.

Manufacturing

CNC shops that can own their stack

Keep control systems supportable, segment shop-floor networks, and build toward auditable machine lifecycle management without binding operations to a disappearing vendor.

CNC applications are a future userspace layer, not a shipped claim
Recording studios

Plug in MIDI. Make music.

Puget Audio is the design-partner environment: mixed-generation Macs, Pis, interfaces, MIDI devices, and low-latency media workflows operated as one understandable system.

Active design direction
Homelab + on-prem

Make the weird fleet coherent

Discover devices, map networks, manage access, and integrate the FOSS services you already trust—without turning the lab into someone else’s cloud.

Mycelium foundation in active development
Shared institutions

Many users. Clear boundaries.

Universities, companies, and nonprofits need role-based access, privacy boundaries, fleet evidence, and graceful operation through disconnected weekends.

Identity and policy primitives evolving
High assurance

Evidence before checkboxes

Build toward DISA STIG baselines and the technical controls that support HIPAA, FedRAMP, and CMMC programs—while keeping deployment and accreditation decisions explicit.

Enablement, not certification
04 / Trust boundaries

Security claims should be inspectable.

fungOS is being designed to produce the controls and evidence serious environments need. It does not make an organization compliant by installation, and this technical preview is not certified for regulated workloads.

IdentityPeople, machines, and services remain distinct principals.
AuthorityRole-based grants define action; discovery never grants trust.
ChangeSigned inputs, deterministic plans, and durable receipts.
ResilienceLocal operation and expiring credentials reduce hard cloud dependencies.
AssuranceSTIG and regulatory-aligned evidence are roadmap work, not present certification.
Early technical preview
